01

The assignment board

A single screen where art requests get routed to the right artist.

What it does high level

The board lists every request waiting for an artist, sorted so the most urgent work sits on top: due date first, then first-come first-served. At a glance it shows:

  • Every waiting request with its comp artwork, due date color coded by urgency, and its complexity tier
  • Each artist's current open workload and the highest complexity they take on
  • An assign dropdown that ranks artists who fit the request's complexity first, lightest workload on top, with type-to-search
  • A one-click detail view of any artist's full plate: their open requests, due dates, and progress
  • A deliberate confirmation step when someone chooses to assign outside the recommended match
102
requests sitting in Needs Assignment today
~380
new art requests per month
13/13
automated tests passing after the hardening pass

Where it stands low level

The board is fully built and tested in the sandbox environment. It went through six rounds of code review with 28 fixes applied, covering accessibility, double-click protection, stale-data races, and permission enforcement. The remaining steps are a team walkthrough and deployment to production for day-to-day use.

Deploy state

Sandbox only, not yet deployed to production.

02

What five months of real requests show

Every number below comes from completed art requests in the Paradies Salesforce org.

The dataset high level

1,900
art requests total since March 10
1,625
completed
792
completed with artist and design direction, analyzed in full
634
of those also carry the finished comp image

All 792 requests were classified into Easy, Medium, and Hard using a rubric drafted from the art team's own descriptions of the work. The result: 59% Easy, 29% Medium, 12% Hard. A second pass reviewed the finished artwork itself on a 52-request sample, and the picture held: text alone and text plus the finished art agreed 81% of the time, with most differences one tier apart.

Method and limits low level

Classification ran against Design_Direction__c, Art_Title__c, and Decoration_Type__c on each record, with the finished comp pulled from the attached file for the image pass. These tiers are a first draft by the AI, not ground truth. The validation step in Section 05 is what turns them into numbers the team can trust. Turnaround timing data from the new date-stamp automation began collecting on July 27 and will be ready to factor into workload balancing after a few more weeks of use.

03

The three complexity tiers, with real examples

Each example below is a real completed request: the original ask and the finished art.

Easy

Text or namedrop only, placing an existing logo, reusing or lightly editing an existing design.

Medium

A new layout from reference or inspiration, icon and text integration, a seasonal redraw, a multi-element composition.

Hard

A brand new illustration or mascot, a photo repaint, large-format or multi-use original art.

*Completed requests with design direction text, per the AI tier draft. The two right-hand columns answer different questions. "Typical mix" is where each artist's work actually concentrates, and is the better guide for routing volume. "Ceiling" is the highest tier with at least three completions, and only answers whether the board should allow that artist to receive work at that tier at all. A high ceiling with a low Hard share, like 150 Easy, 50 Medium, and 5 Hard, describes an Easy-to-Medium workhorse who has occasionally stretched, not a Hard specialist. Note also that the mix reflects what each artist was assigned, not necessarily what they are capable of, which is exactly what the validation step with Wayne resolves. Artists with smaller counts, like Rey Flores at six requests, simply have less data in the system.

05

Phase 2: automatic classification and routing

Decision pending

The plan for new requests to arrive pre-classified with a suggested artist, with a human always making the final call.

How it fits together high level

  • Step 1, validate. Wayne rates about 50 real requests on a prepared rating sheet. The AI's tiers are scored against those answers.
  • Step 2, calibrate. Every disagreement becomes a teaching example for the AI. The rubric is refined and re-scored on a held-out set until agreement is solid.
  • Step 3, wire it in. Once the accuracy holds up, each new art request gets classified as it arrives and the board shows a suggested artist based on who can handle that tier and who has the lightest current load. The team still clicks Assign.
  • Step 4, add speed. As the turnaround timestamps accumulate, suggestions can also weigh who actually completes that tier of work fastest.

What it would cost to run low level

Classification would use Anthropic's Claude Sonnet model, sending the request's direction text plus the reference image and getting back a tier, a confidence level, and a short reason. At current published pricing that is roughly one to two cents per request, which at the current volume of about 380 requests per month comes to around $5 to $8 per month. A smaller model could cut that below $2 per month if the accuracy holds during the pilot. No API spend occurs until the validation step passes and Paradies approves enabling it.

Next step

The validation pass: about thirty minutes with the rating sheet. The scoring and rubric refinement that follow carry no cost.
